steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper on modeling annotator disagreement in subjective tasks like offensiveness rating. Explain why majority-vote labels can be wrong, why target group members' opinions matter, and briefly describe our model and its main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Majority-vote aggregation and why it breaks down for subjective tasks
- Disagreement reflects differences among populations
- Why target group members' opinions matter
- Our model and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Aggregation and subjectivity
  - clear ground truth: multiple labelers + averaging works; near-unanimous agreement -> rest likely inattentive
  - subjective tasks (ground truth varies by person): disagreement-as-noise may not hold
  - e.g. same text offensive to some, not others (Figure 1)
  - recent work questions assumptions of majority-vote labels (cite): single fixed ground truth; aggregation captures it; disagreement = noise not signal; not systematic; aggregation equally suited to straightforward and nuanced tasks
- Disagreement from population differences
  - hate speech detection: disagreement from demographic groups, political parties, not noise (cite)
  - aggregated training -> opinions of minoritized groups w/ more expertise or personal experience overlooked (cite)
- Target group members
  - annotators in the group targeted by a possibly offensive statement often differ from majority of raters
  - relevant lived experience, familiarity with context
  - when/why they differ -> cases where majority is wrong or opinions truly divided
- Our model and results
  - predicts individual annotators' offensiveness ratings + potential target group(s); combines -> target group members' ratings
  - vs baseline w/o individual annotators: +22% individual ratings, +33% variance among annotators, +22% target group aggregate ratings
  - survey responses + demographic features model ratings effectively
  - questions on online experiences -> predict ratings while minimizing intrusive demographic collection

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
For many machine learning tasks where the ground truth is clear, it works well to have multiple people label the examples and then average their judgments: if almost all annotators agree on a label, the others were probably inattentive. But if the task is more subjective, meaning that the ground truth label varies by person, the assumption that disagreement is noise may not hold anymore. For example, the same text may really be offensive to some people and not to others (Figure 1). Recent work has questioned several assumptions behind majority-vote aggregated labels: that there is one fixed ground truth, that the aggregated judgments of a group of annotators capture this ground truth accurately, that disagreement among annotators is noise and not signal, that this disagreement is not systematic, and that aggregation suits very straightforward tasks and more nuanced ones equally well.

In tasks like hate speech detection, annotator disagreement often does not come from noise but from differences among populations, for example demographic groups or political parties. So training on aggregated annotations can lead to the opinions of minoritized groups who have more expertise or personal experience being overlooked.

- Target group members
  - annotators in the group targeted by a possibly offensive statement often differ from majority of raters
  - relevant lived experience, familiarity with context
  - when/why they differ -> cases where majority is wrong or opinions truly divided

- Our model and results
  - predicts individual annotators' offensiveness ratings + potential target group(s); combines -> target group members' ratings
  - vs baseline w/o individual annotators: +22% individual ratings, +33% variance among annotators, +22% target group aggregate ratings
  - survey responses + demographic features model ratings effectively
  - questions on online experiences -> predict ratings while minimizing intrusive demographic collection

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
For many machine learning tasks where the ground truth is clear, it works well to have multiple people label the examples and then average their judgments: if almost all annotators agree on a label, the others were probably inattentive. But if the task is more subjective, meaning that the ground truth label varies by person, the assumption that disagreement is noise may not hold anymore. For example, the same text may really be offensive to some people and not to others (Figure 1). Recent work has questioned several assumptions behind majority-vote aggregated labels: that there is one fixed ground truth, that the aggregated judgments of a group of annotators capture this ground truth accurately, that disagreement among annotators is noise and not signal, that this disagreement is not systematic, and that aggregation suits very straightforward tasks and more nuanced ones equally well.

In tasks like hate speech detection, annotator disagreement often does not come from noise but from differences among populations, for example demographic groups or political parties. So training on aggregated annotations can lead to the opinions of minoritized groups who have more expertise or personal experience being overlooked.

In particular, annotators who belong to the group that is targeted by a possibly offensive statement often have different opinions from the majority of the annotators who rate the text. These annotators may have relevant lived experience or may know the context of the statement better, so understanding when and why their opinions are different from the majority can help to capture cases where the majority is wrong or where opinions really are divided on whether the example is offensive.

We build a model that predicts the ratings of individual annotators on how offensive a text is, and also the potential target group(s) of the text, and then combines this information to predict how target group members rate the offensiveness of the example. Compared to a baseline that does not model individual annotators, we improve performance by 22% at predicting individual annotators' ratings, by 33% at predicting variance among annotators, and by 22% at predicting the aggregate ratings of target group members. We find that annotator survey responses and demographic features let us model ratings effectively, and that survey questions about the online experiences of annotators let us predict their ratings while keeping intrusive collection of demographic information to a minimum.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
For many machine learning tasks in which the ground truth is clear, having multiple people label examples and then averaging their judgments is an effective strategy: if nearly all annotators agree on a label, the rest were likely inattentive. However, the assumption that disagreement is noise may no longer hold if the task is more subjective, in the sense that the ground truth label varies by person. For example, the same text may truly be offensive to some people and not to others (Figure 1). Recent work has questioned several assumptions of majority-vote aggregated labels: that there is a single, fixed ground truth; that the aggregated judgments of a group of annotators accurately capture this ground truth; that disagreement among annotators is noise, not signal; that such disagreement is not systematic; and that aggregation is equally suited to very straightforward tasks and to more nuanced ones [1,2,3,4,5,6].

In tasks such as hate speech detection, annotator disagreement often results not from noise but from differences among populations, e.g., demographic groups or political parties [1,5]. Training with aggregated annotations can thus cause the opinions of minoritized groups with greater expertise or personal experience to be overlooked [4].

In particular, annotators who are members of the group targeted by a possibly offensive statement often differ in their opinions from the majority of annotators who rate the text. Because these annotators may have relevant lived experience or greater familiarity with the context of the statement, understanding when and why their opinions differ from the majority can help capture cases where the majority is wrong or where opinions are truly divided over whether the example is offensive.

We construct a model that predicts individual annotators’ ratings on the offensiveness of text, as well as the potential target group(s) of the text, and combines this information to predict target group members' ratings on the offensiveness of the example. Compared to a baseline that does not model individual annotators, we improve performance by 22% at predicting individual annotators’ ratings, 33% at predicting variance among annotators, and 22% at predicting target group members’ aggregate ratings. We find that annotator survey responses and demographic features allow ratings to be modeled effectively, and that survey questions on annotators’ online experiences allow their ratings to be predicted while minimizing intrusive collection of demographic information.
